# Preface
## To the Favorable Reader.

What the world-renowned Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> once wrote in his *Law* <note>original: "Gesetz." Likely referring to the *Lex Hippocratis*, a brief text outlining the requirements for a successful medical education.</note> regarding the noble **Art of Medicine**: that it is the most excellent of all arts. However, because of the great ignorance of those who practice it, as well as the poor understanding of common folk—who everywhere promote and highly esteem such ignorant people as experienced physicians—it has finally come to the point that, due to such foolish judgments, it is held to be the most wretched of all.

The very same may be said and demonstrated regarding that most praiseworthy art, which is by its nature the most truthful: **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chimie." In the 17th century, the terms chemistry and alchemy were used interchangeably to describe the study of the transformation of matter.</note>, which treats the **Philosopher's Stone**. <note>original Latin: "Lapide Philosophorum." This was the ultimate goal of alchemy: a legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as a universal cure for illness.</note>

For how many have come forward over a great length of time, presenting themselves as great **Chemists**, not only in words but also in writings, who were in truth unwise and foolish fellows—

<meta>catchword: sen/</meta>

<summary>This preface introduces the volume by comparing alchemy to medicine, arguing that both "noble arts" are unfairly disparaged because of the incompetence of fraudulent practitioners and the ignorance of the public. It sets the stage for a defense of "true" chemistry/alchemy against the "foolish fellows" who have tarnished its reputation.</summary>
<keywords>Hippocrates, Art of Medicine, Chemistry, Alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, Lapide Philosophorum, medical ethics, history of science</keywords>

Because of this, the art has been quite unfairly and unwisely attacked by many people, and has been stained by many falsely-invented accusations.

# To the Favorable Reader.

...people are accustomed to spend time devising and practicing **art**. Others believe that the academies and universities are such breeding grounds <note>original: "Seminaria."</note> where not only the <term>Liberal Arts</term> <note>The traditional curriculum of grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note> but also the higher <term>Sciences</term> <note>original: "Scientien."</note> are thoroughly investigated and presented to the youth who are eager for art. This is especially true of <term>Physics</term> <note>In this period, "Physics" referred to natural philosophy—the study of all natural laws and substances—rather than the modern narrow definition.</note>, of which this <term>Chemical Art</term> <note>original: "Chimie-Kunst."</note> is the most distinguished and noble part, and should be regarded as such.

Now, it cannot be denied that at the courts of many great lords, these <term>Chemical Labors</term> <note>original: "Labores Chimici." Alchemical experiments and laboratory work.</note> have been extensively pursued and are still in high practice. However, because no desired effect has resulted from them, it does not follow that the art is false and deceitful. Rather, the demonstrable ignorance regarding the materials—and the manner and way of treating them—blinds the eyes of the <term>Practitioners</term> <note>original: "Laboranten."</note>. They often interpret the beautiful writings of good authors only according to their own whims, or work only according to the literal meaning of the words, and thereby squander noble time and much good money. Is it not testimony enough, the <term>Transmutation</term> <note>The process of changing base metals into gold or silver.</note> performed by the most powerful Emperor **Ferdinand III** in the year 1648—of most glorious memory—with his own hands? Liquid mercury.</note> into solid, good gold, from which...

A more recent transmutation to make gold from tin was witnessed this past year in the Imperial Residence city of Vienna, where a monk named Father Wenzel produced many transmutations <note>original: "tingirt"; literally "tinged," referring to the use of a "tincture" or Philosopher's Stone to change the metal's nature.</note> using a tincture found in his monastery. Thus, this art has been grandly and indeed irrefutably proven many times at the high Imperial Court, even though many discussions and conferences may have occurred there regarding the preparation of that same tincture, and its secrets have not been able to be fully penetrated to this day.

### Preface

Afterward, a special golden coin <note>original: "Numisma"</note>, titled *Divine Transformation* <note>original: "Divina Metamorphosis"</note>, was prepared; as can be seen in more detail in the works of Johann Zwelfer <note>Johann Zwelfer (1618–1668) was an influential physician and apothecary known for his pharmaceutical commentaries.</note> in his *Spagyric Addition* <note>original: "Mantissa Spagyrica"</note>; in the *Oedipus Becheri* <note>A work by Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), a famous German alchemist and physician.</note>; and in the *Golden Calf* <note>original: "guldenen Kalb"</note> of Dr. Schweitzer <note>Johann Friedrich Schweitzer, also known as Helvetius (1630–1709). A more recent transmutation <note>The alchemical process of changing base metals into precious ones.</note> to make gold out of tin was witnessed last year in the Imperial residential city of Vienna. Thus, such an art has been grandly and indeed irreproachably proven many times at the high Imperial Court, even though many discussions <note>original: "Discursen"</note> and conferences may have taken place there regarding the preparation of that same tincture, and to date <note>original: "bis dato"</note> its secret has not yet been able to be penetrated <note>meaning to be understood or reverse-engineered.</note>.

# Johann Wolfgang Dienheim’s Universal Medicine.

## Chapter I.

The daily practice of the medical arts, as well as the diligent application in my studies—linked together as if by a continuous thread through both day and night labor—and also the many travels I have undertaken by water and land for this very purpose, have finally brought me to the point where I can see quite clearly and distinctly that it is indeed possible, by means of a **Universal Medicine** <note>Also known as a Panacea, this was the alchemical "Great Work" believed to cure all diseases and prolong life.</note>, to drive all diseases out of the human body. Indeed, as I hear, it is said that among the **Brahmins** <note>original: *Bragmanern*; the author refers here to the scholarly or priestly class of India</note> and among certain philosophers in the **Kingdom of China**, a custom has persisted since ancient times: that every year on a certain day, as if at a **funeral** <note>original: *Leichbegängniß*</note>, they dress in mourning clothes to weep for the downfall and oblivion of this noble art <note>referring to the "Universal Medicine" or Alchemical art</note>, no differently than for the death of a great prince. They are accustomed to pray for its return from heaven—where they imagine <note>original: *fabuliren*; to tell as a legend or fable</note> it has flown—with voices raised in frequent repetition. I recount this as I have heard it.

Be that as it may, the authors <note>original: *Authores*</note> mentioned above lived in different and widely separated places and at different times, so that it does not seem possible that they could have learned this **error** (as some call it) from one another. Rather, it is evident from this that such a widespread consensus—known not just in one city, but in the entire world—contains and encompasses nothing but the **sun-clear and unadulterated truth**.

## Chapter II.

I know quite well that this **Universal Medicine** <term>Universal Medicine: Also known as the Panacea, this was a hypothetical remedy sought by alchemists that would cure all bodily ailments and indefinitely prolong life.</term> has been mockingly criticized and debunked by various highly learned and honorable men. If one carefully reflects upon and considers those conditions which—according to the rules of the Sages <note>original: *Weltweisen*; referring to the "Sophic" tradition or natural philosophers.</note>—the matter <note>original: *Materi*</note> of the **Universal Medicine** <term>Universal-Arzney: Also known as the Panacea or Elixir of Life, this was the ultimate goal of alchemical medicine, believed to cure all ailments by restoring the body's fundamental balance.</term> must possess, one must conclude from infallible grounds and evidence that it is nothing other, nor can it be anything other, than the **elements** <note>original: *Elementa*</note> themselves.

...have called our **medicine**, and I do not know whether they did so to hide the matter or to explain it more clearly. What is certain is that they cause more darkness than light, so that a whole host of names—which the world still possesses today—has sprouted from it. Almost everyone who has made a little progress in this art, or at least imagines they have, invents new names, new <term>characters</term> <note>original: *Characteres*; these are the shorthand symbols or sigils used by alchemists to represent substances.</note> or signs, and new representations according to their own whim. 

The ancients, however, always made it a practice to use the names of the gods and goddesses, and especially those of the **planets**. But God preserve us! What errors, what abuses, what foolishness has sprung from this? How miserably have our newcomers depicted the highly learned inventions of the ancients? How far have they wandered from the ancient meaning? 

To them, **Jupiter** signifies tin; **Saturn** lead; **Mercury** quicksilver; and gold, silver, ore, and steel they call the **Sun**, **Moon**, **Venus**, and **Mars**. What kind of darkness is this? ### Chapter XIII.

It is now time for us to respond to the objections of our opponents. They say that there are four qualities and properties in the human body which correspond, both in number and in nature, with the four elements <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>. Now, however, each of these aforementioned qualities has its own particular corruptions <note>In the medical context of the 1600s, "corruptions" refers to diseases or imbalances of the bodily humors.</note> that are directly opposed and contrary to the other three. Therefore, they argue, there must necessarily be at least as many kinds of medicinal remedies, so that each quality may be cured by a remedy that is set against it and is its opposite <note>This refers to the traditional medical principle of *contraria contrariis curantur*—the idea that a "hot" disease (like a fever) must be treated with a "cold" medicine.</note>.

To these people I respond as follows: I do not deny that for different illnesses one must use different medicines, according to the nature of each disease; rather, I say and maintain that these same medicines—though they be many and varied—can be sharpened and enhanced through the power of a **Universal Medicine** <term>Universal Medicine: Also known as the Panacea or the Elixir of Life in alchemy, it was believed to be a supreme substance that could bolster the body's vital force, making all other specific cures more effective.</term>, so that they may perform their effect and operation all the more surely. If they consider this impossible, let them take care that they do not hold their erroneous opinion of healing—which is supposed to happen through **contraries** <note>original: "contraria"</note> or opposing things—all too...

## Chapter XVI.

It is now time that we—having finished the discourse in which we demonstrated the truth of the Universal Medicine <note>The "Panacea" or "Philosopher's Stone" in its medicinal form, believed to cure all ailments and prolong life</note>, as well as its ease and readiness, and proved its material—should also add a few words regarding its utility and use.

### Chapter XVII.

The liver commonly suffers because of heat and warmth, but sometimes also because of frost and cold; the former is accompanied by a drought or dryness, while the latter is accompanied by an excess of moisture, though occasionally—yet more rarely—this latter condition alone can cause a grievance. # Chapter XVIII.

The lung is to the heart as a cushion and a valve; and it was created not only for comfort—as some wrongly believe—but also out of necessity. Without the lungs, the <term>natural heat</term> <note>The "vital heat" believed by early physicians to be generated in the heart to sustain life.</note> would have no material to sustain itself; indeed, it would cease and vanish, just as a fire is extinguished by smothering because it has no air, which Aristotle called the "food" of fire. Furthermore, the heart itself, as the seat of this natural heat, would easily break during its constant pulsing by striking against the hard parts of the body if it did not have the soft covering of the lungs, even if the natural heat were still present. 

Now, these lungs are often unable to perform their office because they are hindered either by moisture and cold, or by heat and excessive dryness. In such illnesses, wine, mead, and other drinks mixed with white rock candy <note>original: *Candelzucker*</note> are used with great benefit. ## Chapter XX.

Emperor Trajan, who was as highly skilled in medicine as he was in law, was accustomed to comparing the spleen to a treasury; for just as when the spleen increases in size, the other limbs and internal organs decrease, and conversely, when the spleen decreases, the remaining parts of the body usually increase. This same relationship exists with a treasury in a republic. For the goods of the common citizens are drained when the treasury bulges and is puffed up with money, being filled by means of customs, tithes, and a thousand other types of taxes from the citizens' money. In my opinion, this happens with the spleen because it draws too much "earthly moisture" <note>In the humoral system, "earthly moisture" refers to black bile, which is cold and dry</note> into itself. For although nature has wisely provided that the good blood be separated from the **melancholic juices** <note>The "melancholic juices" refer to black bile, one of the four humors, which the spleen was thought to filter from the blood</note> by the office of the spleen, yet when the spleen draws either all or most of these to itself, nourishment is simultaneously withdrawn from the limbs. This is because the remaining blood—once the melancholic part has been drawn away—becomes far too **spirited** and **subtle** <note>original: *subtil*; in this context, it means the blood becomes too thin or airy to provide physical substance to the body</note>, and thus cannot stand firm on its own. Or, it happens because the spleen, on account of its increase and the resulting **obstruction** <note>original: *Verstopffung*; a blockage of the "passages" or "vessels" that prevents the flow of humors</note> of the same...

# Universal Medicine.

->77<-

The patient's age and gender, as well as the season in which this **medicine** is used, must be carefully considered. Based on these factors, the common medications with which our **medicine** is mixed should be prescribed in the measure and weight that is suitable to be given to that specific person, at that age, and at that time. According to the common measures and weights of medications, the dose and weight of our **Universal Medicine** <term>Universal-Arzney: a "cure-all" substance sought by alchemists to treat all diseases by restoring balance to the body</term> must also be measured.

For example: if a **decoction** <note>original: *abgesottenes Wasser*; literally "boiled-down water," referring to a medicinal broth or herbal tea</note> made from a full pound of those herbs most useful for a person's illness is given to an otherwise strong man, then a full **scruple** <term>Scrupel: an apothecary weight equal to 20 grains, or about 1.3 grams</term> or a third of a **drachm** <term>Quintlein: also known as a dram, a small unit of weight; three scruples make one drachm</term> can certainly be given along with the prescribed decoction.

However, if one were to give a weaker person only half a pound of the liquid, it would be enough to mix in only half a **scruple** or ten **grains** <term>Gran: the smallest unit of apothecary weight, originally based on the weight of a single grain of wheat or barley</term> of our **Universal Medicine**.

If three **ounces** <term>Untzen: a standard unit of weight; in the apothecary system, twelve ounces typically made one pound</term> or six **loth** <term>Loth: a traditional German unit of weight, usually equivalent to half an ounce or approximately 14.5 to 17 grams</term> are sufficient, then it is also enough to add only five **grains** of our medicine to those six **loth** of decoction; this proportion seems to be neither too strong nor too weak.

The same principle applies to other medicines, which should follow this same rule, as it would be unnecessary to list every single possible weight. Thus, what we have written thus far...

# Chapter 25.

Those who, despite such a bright light, still remain blind and hold it to be an impossible thing to make **gold** through the **alchemical art** <term>original: *Chymische Kunst*; during this period, chemistry and alchemy were not yet separate disciplines</term> / primarily use these reasons and **logical arguments** <term>original: *Vernunfft-Schlüsse*; referring to formal syllogisms used in scholarly debate</term> to maintain their opinion and overturn all experience. They say / that among those who have applied themselves most diligently, very few / indeed perhaps none are found / who can make **gold** through art: Now, it would be necessary / that if the art were true and proven / it would either always or at least for the most part reach and bring forth its **effect** <note>original: *Effect*</note> and action. Therefore, **alchemy** / which is called an art of making **gold** / if it were capable of anything in this regard / would reach its **effect** either always or at least commonly / and because it does not do so / it follows necessarily / that by its nature / it is nothing / and has no power nor might / to make **gold** or **silver** ; because that which does not exist / or has no essence / as we say / can also have no properties. Furthermore / the **alchemical** art is either a natural **potential** <term>original: *Potentia*; a latent power or capacity</term> and power / or an **acquired habit** <term>original: *Habitus*; a learned disposition or skill</term> ; if it is the first / then it is common to all men ; if it is the second / then it performs its work quickly / easily and commonly.

<meta>This page continues the logical arguments against alchemy. Having previously defined alchemy as either a natural potential or an acquired habit, the author now argues it possesses neither quality, citing scholarly authorities like Cardano and Aquinas to prove why the artificial creation of gold is impossible.</meta>

->Universal Medicine.<-

Now, however, alchemy lacks both <note>Referring to the previous page's distinction: alchemy is neither a natural power common to all men nor a learned skill that produces results easily.</note>: Therefore, not only can no gold be made by means of it, but it cannot in any way be called an art. Thirdly, those things that differ from one another in species and are distinguished from one another by their own **substantial form** <term>original: *selbst-ständigen Form*; in the philosophy of the time, this refers to the essential nature that makes a substance what it is</term> cannot be transformed into one another.

Fourthly, three things are necessarily required for the generation of **perfect things**: namely, one that acts or works <note>the active agent</note>, one which is acted upon <note>the passive matter</note>, and then also the **place** itself where the generation occurs; it is different, however, in the case of imperfect things. Now, gold is the most perfect of all metals: therefore, these three things are also required for the generation of gold. Even if we assume that the alchemists can have that which acts or works, and likewise the passive matter of gold, they still cannot in any way have the **place** where gold is generated, because that place is deep within the earth.

And these reasons and logical proofs are cited by **Chassaneus** in his *Catalog of the World’s Glory* <note>original: *Verzeichniß der Welt Ehre*; referring to Barthélemy de Chasseneuz's *Catalogus gloriae mundi* (1529)</note>, **Cardanus** in *On the Variety of Things* <note>original: *von der Dinge Manchfaltigkeit*; referring to Girolamo Cardano's *De rerum varietate* (1557)</note> in the tenth book, fifty-first chapter. Also in *The Golden Bracelet* <note>original: *Das Gultene Armband*; likely referring to a common legal or theological reference work of the period</note>, under the word **Alchemy**; **Gregorius de Valentia** in the sixth disputation of the second part of **Saint Thomas** <note>referring to comments on the *Summa Theologica* of Thomas Aquinas</note> in the thirteenth question, concerning vain observations; and **Petrus Binsfeldius** in his **Commentary**— <note>The text breaks here; Binsfeld was a prominent theologian and bishop of Trier known for his writings on witchcraft and legal theology.</note>

...commentary on the Title in the Code concerning Sorcerers and Mathematicians <note>original: "Tit. <meta>This page continues the defense of alchemy against the legal and theological attacks mentioned on the previous page. # Page 87
### Universal Medicine <term>Universal-Artzney: The "Universal Medicine" or Panacea, a legendary substance in alchemy capable of curing all diseases and perfecting "sick" (base) metals into gold.</term>

Concerning now the first line of reasoning from our opponents—since they believe that the art of alchemy <term>Alchymie-Kunst: the practice of attempting to transform base metals into noble ones</term> is worth nothing for this reason, and can achieve or do nothing in the transformation of metals, because every art either always or at least commonly achieves its intended effect, while alchemy for the most part fails and very rarely reaches its goal and purpose—the answer to this is that while the first premise <note>The "first premise" refers to the idea that a valid art should produce consistent results.</note> is undoubtedly true, the second premise takes as certain something that should first have been proven through rational conclusions. For it is false that alchemy has ever deceived its true practitioners, and even less true that it does so always or commonly.

That false and ignorant chemists have suffered punishment due to their lack of understanding and ignorance, and have seen their hopes go unfulfilled, is something I well believe. However, one must not conclude from this that the art itself is false simply because those unskilled in it cannot practice the very art they do not understand. This is no different than if someone wanted to deny that astronomy <term>Sternseher-Kunst: literally "star-seer art," referring to both astronomy and astrology, which were not strictly separated at the time</term>, arithmetic <term>Rechen-Kunst: the art of calculation</term>, and music were true arts because a peasant does not understand music, cannot calculate, or knows nothing of the orbits of the heavenly spheres. Indeed, those chemists who call themselves chemists today are even less like true chemists than a peasant is like an astronomer...

Yet things, even if they differ in species, may nonetheless not be entirely different, but of one kind, differing from one another only in their effects. # Universal Medicine.

F v

and the other metals behave toward gold and silver. For whatever properties gold has—namely, melting, allowing itself to be drawn out or beaten with a hammer or tongs, being heavy, shining, and resisting fire—the other metals also have these same properties, though in a corrupted, maimed, and (to put it more clearly) less perfect way. They do indeed shine; they are heavy; they resist fire—but not as intensely or as long as gold. They can be drawn out and beaten, but not as thin. They melt, but not completely, or at least not as quickly or as easily. Therefore, like all other imperfect things, they can be raised and advanced to their proper perfection. However, this is accomplished not so much by art—which acts only *organically* <note>original: *organicè*; here meaning that human "Art" or technology acts only as a tool or instrument for Nature's own processes</note>—but primarily by Nature itself. This is no different than a *physician* <note>original: *Medicus*</note>, who with all his skill performs, does, and undertakes nothing other than to assist Nature so that she may rightly carry out her natural functions. He does this by removing obstacles and adding what seems most useful to strengthen weak Nature. Not to mention those ducks or other Indian birds <note>This refers to the "Barnacle Goose" myth, a common belief in early modern natural history that certain birds grew from trees or driftwood. ### Universal Medicine.

Logical reasoning and experience have proven that this can not only happen according to the ordinary course of Nature, but that it actually occurs? How could such a thing be dangerous or harmful to a Commonwealth <note>original: *Republic*; used here in the classical sense of the state or the public good</note>, when no man who knows and understands what exists (or can exist) in Nature doubts its utility? For this reason, it is not only desired by a single city, but is eagerly wished for, laboriously sought, and craved at great expense by the entire world.

Do they perhaps suspect some danger or harm because chemists <note>original: *Chymisten*; referring to alchemists and early chemical practitioners</note> use poisons and other corrosive <note>original: *fressende*; literally "eating," describing caustic substances like acids</note> substances for this work? However, nowadays such corrosive and poisonous substances are not only found in all pharmacies <term>pharmacies: *Apothecken*; shops where medicinal compounds, including chemical ones, were prepared and sold</term>, but are also frequently mixed into other medicines. Therefore, all pharmacies would necessarily have to bring great danger and harm to a Commonwealth. To this I also add that true alchemists use such corrosive and poisonous substances either not at all, or only very rarely.

Or is it considered harmful because alchemists are commonly heretics? However, even this is not true. should build no more vineyards in the future, or bring wine to us from other places—as *Tacitus* <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian who wrote about the Germanic tribes</note> writes that the Germans used to do in ancient times—simply because wine is so greatly misused, and so many and cruel vices spring daily from the abuse of wine, namely from drunkenness and excessive drinking? # Conclusion.

There will be some who might wish for an actual description and **process**—namely, how our recognized **matter** <note>original: "Materi"; refers to the *Materia Prima* or the base substance required to begin the alchemical work</note> should be **prepared** and made, so that from it either the **Philosophical Gold-Stone** <note>The author uses a specific term here, likely identifying the Philosophers' Stone by its ability to produce gold</note> or our **Universal Medicine** <note>Also known as the Panacea, a legendary substance capable of curing all ailments</note> might come. Regarding this **Raymund** <note>Refers to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a celebrated philosopher and alchemist often cited in these manuscripts.</note> says / that the manner of **ceration** <note>The process of bringing a substance to a waxy state.</note> is / that the sublimation of the reserved moist parts be repeated and begun over the stone so many times / that the stone is circulated with its own root-like, remaining moisture / which never leaves its body in the mixture / until the right liquidity is reached.

# Anonymi

Through work, the <term>body <note>original: *Cörper*; the solid material or "matter" being worked on in the alchemical vessel.</note></term> is broken apart / destroyed / made subtle / and diligently governed / until its subtle <term>soul <note>original: *Seele*; the essential, volatile life-force believed to reside within matter.</note></term> is drawn out from its thickness / and converted into a thin, subtle, and incomprehensible <term>spirit <note>original: *Geist*; a vaporous or refined state of the substance.</note></term> / then the body is converted into an incorporeal thing / and the incorporeal into a body / and this is the true and most truthful discovery and rule of working. 

And accordingly, it is to be known / that every body is dissolved by a sharp spirit / with which it is mixed / and to which, without any doubt, it is made equal and spiritual. And when this spirit is sublimated / it is called the water / which washes and cleanses itself / as was said before / in that it rises / with its most subtle essence / and leaves behind its corrupting parts. And this rising the <term>philosophers <note>original: *Philosophi*; here referring specifically to alchemists or "natural philosophers."</note></term> have called <term>distillation <note>original: *Destillacion*; the process of purifying a liquid by heating it into vapor and condensing it back into liquid.</note></term> / washing / and <term>sublimation <note>original: *Sublimacion*; the transition of a substance directly from a solid to a gas phase, used here to describe the purification of the "stone."</note></term>. 

Therefore / when the perfect sublimation is brought to an end / then the stone is made alive with its life-giving spirit / or natural soul / of which it had been deprived in the <term>blackness <note>original: *Schwärtze*; the *nigredo* stage, characterized by decay and the "death" of the material.</note></term> / and is breathed into / ensouled / awakened again / brought back and led to the final end / of all subtleness and purity / and elevated from the bottom of the vessel / into a crystalline snow-white stone / which clings to the sides of the aforementioned vessel / and the <term>dregs <note>original: *feces*; the impure solid remains or waste left at the bottom after a process.</note></term> of the same remain at the very bottom of the vessel. ...from the dregs <note>original: *fecibus*; the waste matter or sediment left behind during chemical processes.</note> / and set it apart / and sublimate it without those same dregs: for if you venture to sublimate it with the dregs / you will never bring them together for all eternity / and you will lose your labor. <image-desc>An octagonal woodcut serving as a decorative initial 'D'. It depicts a man (Saturn) holding a scythe and a bundle of plants or wood.</image-desc>
You might ask, my brotherly friend, where or from whence we might find the Water or Magistery of the Wise? For Geber <note>original: *Geber*; likely referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century father of Arab chemistry.</note> says: "Our water is a cloud-water." But Aristotle says: "Our water is a dry water." <note>Aristotle was frequently cited by alchemists to lend philosophical authority to the idea of "Dry Water"—a paradox describing a substance that behaves like a liquid but does not wet the hands.</note> Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of the Hermetic arts.</note> reports: "Our water is collected from a foul menstrual matter." Danthynus mentions: "Our water is found in all stables, privies, and stinking puddles." And Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> desires that our water grow in the mountains and valleys. **Note Well.** But the fools do not understand these words and take such things to be common Mercury <note>original: *Mercurium*; refers to quicksilver.</note>. It is not Mercury, however, but rather a **dry water** which provides an "entrance" <term>ingress; the ability of an alchemical substance to penetrate and transform a metal</term> and unites all mineral spirits, soul, and body together. # Preface.

...[compo]sition of the two preceding bodies, which were implanted in it by **GOD**: So that these three salts <note>original: *Saltz*; in alchemical philosophy, "Salt" represents the principle of fixity and the physical body of a substance</note> are kept hidden within the mentioned earth. To a wise man, this little bit should be enough; you will learn more from the following parts <note>original Latin: *Theilibus*</note>, and you will have bright Nature standing right before your door, completely revealed and recognized.

## Hermetic Theses.

### I.

He who does not believe in the possibility of the divine Hermetic Work <note>The "Hermetic Work" or *Opus Magnum* refers to the alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone or attaining spiritual perfection.</note>, who does not know its essence, or who despises it, has not yet worshiped the majesty of the great **GOD**, nor satisfied the requirements of Nature. Between Sun and Moon, we consider that man to be blind who is enlightened neither by the rays of Divine Grace nor by the Light of Nature <note>original: *Liecht der Natur*; a Paracelsian concept referring to innate human reason and the knowledge gained from observing the natural world.</note>. For why should the Philosophers <note>original: *Weltweisen*; literally "world-wise ones," a common term for alchemists and natural philosophers.</note> have regarded this work as a gift from **GOD** and equal to the birth of animals, if they had not believed that it depends on both Principles <note>original: *Principiis*; likely referring to the fundamental alchemical dualities such as Sulfur and Mercury or the Divine and the Natural.</note>? Since even simple peasants <note>original: *Bauren*; farmers or commoners often used in alchemical texts as a contrast to "sophisticated" but misguided scholars.</note> are not unaware that **GOD** and Nature—who both flee solitude—have granted to all things their own seminal perpetuation through their alternation. What, then, might the Philosophers and seekers of secret things not accomplish?

### II.

Only the Sophists <note>original: *Sophisten*; in this context, it refers to "false alchemists" or those who use trickery and logic rather than true spiritual and natural understanding.</note>, who believe they can [attain] to perfect... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

knowledge of this secret attained; the ignorant, by following the darkness, have recognized either only one principle <note>original: *Principium*; in alchemy, this usually refers to the fundamental components of matter, such as the Three Principles (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury) or the duality of the Divine and the Natural.</note> or perhaps none at all. Therefore, because they denied honor to one and capability to the other—after shamefully breaking the alliance with both and transgressing the laws of Nature—they have stained the pure with the impure, bringing forth nothing other than a monstrosity. And so, following their own whims while disregarding and misunderstanding the name of the Paracelsian Electrum <note>original: *Electri*; in the works of Paracelsus, "Electrum" refers to a powerful alloy of the seven planetary metals, believed to possess celestial virtues.</note>, they have sought our Work quite blindly. They did not look toward its true purpose, namely the glory of **GOD**. In the end, because they lived chimerically <note>original: *Chimerisch*; acting on delusions or pursuing impossible, multi-headed fantasies like the mythical Chimera.</note>, they gathered nothing but smoke, suffered the loss of their wealth, and now experience shame, which they must mourn most painfully.

### III.

Several more subtle minds, who differ somewhat from the sophists <note>The author uses "sophists" to describe "puffers" or false alchemists who use complex but empty logic rather than true spiritual and natural insight.</note>, have recognized the true matter of the philosophical work; however, they have not been able to make use of it. The reason for this was that they read first this author <note>original: *Authorem*.</note> and then that one, seeking profit from them. But because the ancients prepared this matter in one way, and the moderns in another—some indeed with great effort and danger, while others by more certain and shorter [ways]—

Therefore, they seek among the ancients the manner of the <term>solutions</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid substance into a liquid state, a fundamental early step in alchemy.</note>: from Lully <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy.</note> the weights: from Avicenna <note>The Persian physician Ibn Sina (980–1037); his works were foundational to both medicine and alchemical theory.</note> the <term>fermentations</term> <note>A stage where the alchemical substance is matured or multiplied in power, similar to how leaven acts on dough.</note>: from Bernard of Trevisan the fire: from Paracelsus the <term>projections</term> <note>The final stage of the Great Work, where the Philosopher's Stone is "cast" upon base metals to transmute them into gold or silver.</note>, and so forth. Therefore, if you do not find in Lully that which is in Geber; nor in Morienus that which is in Arnold of Villanova; nor in Paracelsus that which you find in others: you should not accuse one or the other. For they have all reached a single goal through different means, although working within one matter.

### IV.

But if fortune favors you, and you are a diligent follower of Nature, then everything will proceed according to your wish; and Nature—a servant of the infinite Majesty—will, through Divine help, provide assistance to your work. Therefore, follow this same teacher; imitate her; and diligently investigate the causes, matter, motions, and <note>original: *End-Ursach*; the "final cause" or ultimate purpose of a process.</note> **final cause** of the Work. However, everything that has successfully proceeded for you, you should apply to the honor of the Triune **GOD** and for the benefit of your neighbor. For in this is established the true purpose of the <term>world-wise</term> <note>original: *Weltweisen*; a common German term for philosophers or sages who study the secrets of the natural world.</note>.

### V.

As I now prepare to address the universal <term>Magisterium</term> <note>Also known as the "Great Work" or the "Mastery," the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> of the sages (which God Most High has bestowed upon mortal men out of pure grace) as a medicine against all illnesses and defects, I wish to touch upon it briefly in a shorter way, more agreeable to Nature, and with such sincerity that no one before me has more clearly made known this gift of God to posterity. For what I have learned without deceit, I share with others without envy.

Above all, however, you must completely banish from your mind all the follies of the <term>sophists</term> <note>In alchemical literature, "sophists" or "puffers" were those who pursued chemical experiments without understanding the true, natural philosophy, often leading to wasted effort and "fictions."</note>, including their **fictions** and **fixations**, **sublimations**, **congealations**, **amalgamations**, and the **precipitations** of mercuries, antimonies, salts, and tartars, as well as the distillations and preparations of herbs and animals, etc., to which such sophists and misguided people are devoted. Instead, you must proceed by the shortest and surest path of Nature.

## MATTER.

### VI.

Now, I shall begin with the parts that constitute our Mastery, and especially with the **Matter**, in the investigation of which almost countless seekers have in vain **labored.** <note>original: *mühet*; completing the thought from the catchword.</note>

# D. Huginus à Barma,

only recounted with different words in the first book of his *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarii*; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a seminal 13th-century alchemical text often attributed to Arnoldus de Villa Nova.</note>, in the seventh chapter, where he says: Our medicine is drawn from those things in which it already exists.

### VIII.

Again, *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founding figure of the alchemical tradition.</note> has shown elsewhere how to extract such a substance from the earthly planets <note>In alchemical code, "planets" refers to the seven metals of antiquity.</note> or perfect metals, saying: Gold and silver are the roots of this art. For this reason, the son of *Hamuel* <note>Likely referring to an Arabic alchemical authority, such as Hali or Hamuel.</note> taught that the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original Latin: *Lapis Philosophorum*; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note> is a water coagulated in gold and silver. *Trevisanus* <note>Bernard of Treviso, a 15th-century alchemist famous for his lifelong quest for the Stone.</note> reports: there are two mercurial substances originating from a single root. *Geber* <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry."</note>, according to *Zacharia* <note>Likely referring to the French alchemist Denis Zachaire.</note>, says: it is a viscous water, joined together through the action of its metallic sulfur. *Paracelsus* in his book, *On the Transmutation of Metals*, in the thirteenth chapter, reports: It is an <term>Electrum</term> <note>A naturally occurring or alchemical alloy of gold and silver.</note> or <term>Cinnabar</term> <note>original: *Zinober*; the bright red mineral form of mercury sulfide, central to many alchemical processes.</note>, which is to say, a composition of two minerals, sulfur and mercury; saying: an *Electrum* is nothing other than a mixture of two, three, or more minerals or metals. Why then should the <term>Sulfur of the Sun</term> <note>original: *Sulphur Solis*; the active, "masculine" principle extracted from gold.</note> joined together in a philosophical manner with the <term>Mercury of the Moon</term> <note>original: *Mercurio Lunæ*; the passive, "feminine" principle extracted from silver.</note> not be an *Electrum* or a *Cinnabar*? And truly, one lion begets another, just as giants are born from giants; and no eagle will ever lay a dove’s egg.

### IX.

Just as a man and a woman are not capable of procreation without the seeds of both; so also this man of ours, gold, and the woman, silver, cannot conceive at all without the seeds of both. Therefore, the *Philosophers* <note>original: *Philosophi*; referring to the collective lineage of alchemical masters.</note> have finally concluded that a third must necessarily be present: the life-giving and *chemical* seeds of both the man and the woman, without which the entire work will be in vain. Such a seed, however, is solely our *Mercury* <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> or *Evestrum* <note>A term from Paracelsian philosophy referring to a prophetic or astral spirit; here it describes the eternal, subtle essence found within the elements.</note>, which is to say: the perpetual and eternal thing contained within the elements of the world, and the purest spirit which transforms the whole world. I shall specifically and clearly demonstrate its nature, origin, preparation, and use, as well as those of all other principles.

### XII.

Our Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius*; the "Mercury of the Philosophers," a spiritual substance rather than the common liquid metal.</note> is very pure, without any stains, white and red, and was called the "Paradise-Water" by Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541).</note> as well as by Isaac <note>likely referring to Isaac Hollandus, a renowned alchemical author.</note>. And this is not without reason: for it moistens the entire rim of the earth and is spread out far and wide into four great springs <note>A reference to the four rivers of Eden (Genesis 2:10-14).</note>, and generates its powers in the **threefold kingdom** <note>The three kingdoms of nature: Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral.</note>. (If you understand this, then you understand the whole work.) If you seek more understanding of this, you will find it in the **philosophical resolution** <note>original: *Resolution*; the process of dissolving or breaking a substance down into its fundamental parts.</note> of every single thing: for the last thing of Nature according to our science is the first thing of Nature itself.

### XIII.

This *philosophical Mercury* is dry and moist, is volatile and fixed, composed in such a proportion that only the **Children of Hermes** <note>A traditional name for alchemists, followers of Hermes Trismegistus.</note> can distinguish one from the other. The Philosophers have observed its earthly husks, seeing how clear and transparent they are, and marveled that in such a snow-whiteness, such a high redness lies hidden. Therefore, they have also called it "the Heaven," not only because it contains within itself universal Nature, but because it receives from all things their *astra* <note>original: *astra*; the "stars" or celestial, vital sparks within matter</note> or innermost essence and their movements. # The Saturnian Kingdom.

...you must separate through frequent **calcination** <note>original: *Calcinirung*; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder.</note> and **solutions** <note>original: *Solvirungen*; the act of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note>, which labors in this work are called the first **sublimations** <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to describe the refinement of Mercury.</note> of **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurii*; the transformative, fluid principle in alchemy.</note>. ### XVI.

This thus prepared and purified body is called by **Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541).</note> an **Ostrich’s Stomach** <note>original: *Strauß Magen*; a metaphor for a powerful digestive fire or solvent capable of "digesting" (dissolving) even the hardest metals, just as the ostrich was legendary for being able to eat and digest iron.</note> that emerges from the earth, and its spirit is called the spirit of the ostrich growing in the earth. In order that you might obtain this, lead the ostrich into its previous **Chaos** <note>The primal, unorganized state of matter from which the philosopher's stone is born.</note> in which it lay hidden, and in which the elements—as if in a hidden dungeon or cave—have secretly held this wondrous spirit of life, a true **Panurgus** <note>original: *Panurgum*; a Greek-derived term for an "all-worker" or universal agent.</note> and **Proteus** <note>original: *Protheum*; after the Greek sea-god who could change his shape at will, representing the transformative nature of the substance.</note>. This spirit is the **Lunaria** <note>Moon-plant or lunar essence.</note> of **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a major figure in alchemical literature.</note>; the **Dragon’s Blood** <note>original: *Drachen-Blut*; a common alchemical term for a deep red substance or "secret fire."</note> of **Albertus Magnus**; the **Saturnian Water** <note>original: *Saturnische Wasser*; a term for the "dissolving water" associated with the leaden or Saturnine stage of alchemy.</note> of **Basilius**; the **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: *Weingeist*; here used metaphorically to describe a pure, volatile essence, not necessarily common alcohol.</note> of **Arnoldus**; but by its true, right name it is called the **true Philosophical Mercury**, the **sourest vinegar**, the **Virgin’s Milk** <note>original: *Jungfrau-Milch*; a term for a white, nourishing mercurial liquid.</note>, the **sharp water**, the **dry water** which does not wet any hand.

# From Huginus à Barma

So that we do not now neglect the **vessels** <term>vessels: the containers, usually glass, used to hold the chemical materials</term> of the first **Herculean labor** <note>original: "Herculischen Arbeit"; a common alchemical metaphor for the difficult stages of the Great Work</note>, you should know that two kinds are necessary. The **Philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the historical lineage of alchemists like Hermes Trismegistus or Geber</note> mention these often, and within them, they accomplish the entire work. The first is called the vessel of Art; the other, the vessel of Nature.

->LXIII.<-

The vessel of Art is a **philosophical egg** <term>philosophical egg: a round, long-necked glass flask (a bolthead) that is sealed to create a closed system</term> blown from pure glass. It has the shape of an egg with a neck that is not too long, and its topmost part must be **hermetically** sealed. It must be of such a size that the **matter** <note>original: "Materie"; the raw chemical substance being transformed</note> fills only one-fourth of it. For the matter requires a sufficient space to complete its **circulations** <note>original: "Circulationes"; the process of a substance evaporating and condensing back down in a continuous cycle</note>, while the **mercurial dew** <note>original: "mercurialische Thau"; the vaporized essence of the substance</note> is moved by the external heat, rising and descending. Through such back-and-forth movements, there occur the **sublimations** <note>original: "Sublimationes"</note>, the **imbibitions** <note>original: "Imbibitiones"; the process of a solid absorbing a liquid</note>, the **irrorations** <note>original: "Irrorationes"; a light moistening or sprinkling of the matter</note>, the **precipitations** <note>original: "Praecipitationes"</note>, the **cohobations** <note>original: "Cohobationes"; the pouring of a distilled liquid back onto the solid remains to extract more essence</note>, the **separations** <note>original: "Separationes"</note> of the elements, the **digestions** <note>original: "Digestiones"; the softening or maturing of a substance through steady, gentle heat</note>, and so on. Regarding these, the Philosophers have written so many different chapters so that the **sophists** <note>original: "Sophisten"; refers to fraudulent alchemists or those who lack true understanding</note> might be deceived. For the work is not accomplished in many different vessels, but in one single and simple fire.

# Preface.

**M**en are accustomed to say in the common proverb: **He who distinguishes well, teaches well** <note>original Latin: *Qui benè distinguit, benè docet*</note>. This, however, does not happen among the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists, the "philosophers of nature."</note> in their alchemical books—which are least of all written **methodically**. For they sometimes treat the last things first and the first things last, thereby **confusing** and distressing the reader, so that he gains little improvement from the reading of such books. **Mercury** is mostly to blame for this, as the reader assumes that there is only one kind. Yet the <term>Philosophers</term> say: "Our gold is not common gold; our silver is not common silver; and our **mercury** is not the common mercury." For common gold and silver are dead, but ours is living. Thus the <term>Philosophers</term> admit that besides common quicksilver there is another, thereby creating a twofold mercurial substance. # I.

## On *Mercury* in General / and What *Azoth* Is.

The Philosophers call their <term>Mercury</term> <note>the "Philosophical Mercury," a universal principle of fluidity and transformation, not common quicksilver</note> *Mercury Azoth*, which is a very thought-provoking word; for the *A.* is the beginning of all four major languages / and is called *Alpha* in Greek, and *Aleph* in Hebrew. Likewise, the *Z* is the last letter in German and Latin; the *O.* is called *Omega* by the Greeks, and is the last letter in their alphabet; the *Th.* is called *Tav* <note>original: *Thav*</note> in Hebrew, and is likewise the last letter in their alphabet / or *Aleph-Beth*. Thus, it can be called *Azoth*, the *A.* and the *O.*, the beginning and the end / understood as the alphabet, <note>original: *Apoc. 22. v. 14.* and *Apoc. 1. v. 11.*</note> Revelation 22:13—the first and the last—and Revelation 1:11. Now the beginning and the end / the head and the tail / the <term>Head and Tail of the Dragon</term> <note>original: *Caput* and *Cauda Draconis*; points of intersection in astronomy, but here used to symbolize the complete cycle of the alchemical process, often depicted as a serpent eating its own tail</note>, have the middle enclosed within them / and for this reason <term>Mercury</term> is called a dragon by <note>Richard the Englishman (Richardus Anglicus), a 13th-century physician and alchemical writer</note> *Rich. Angl.* book 2, chapter 14, adorned upon the head with a crown; because the head is the golden <term>sulfur</term> <note>the active, solar, or "fiery" principle in alchemy</note> and the tail is the earth / about which the Philosophers write: Turn the head to the tail / and you have the art entire. And *Belmontius* <note>likely an alchemical authority or pseudonym</note> says: <note>original: *Mercurius est Draco Magnus*</note> Mercury is the Great Dragon,

### VII. Lyncurium.

The precious stone **Lyncurium** <note>original: "Lyncurer," a legendary gemstone once believed to be solidified lynx urine, often identified by modern scholars as amber or zircon</note>, called *Leshem* in Hebrew, originates from the urine that lynxes discharge and then scrape into and cover with earth, as Pliny writes in Book 37, chapters 2 and 3, and Book 8, chapter 38. ### Regarding the / or those Matters / and Ingredients / constituting the Philosopher's Stone.

### XIX.

## Of Tartar <note>original: *Tartaro*</note>, Wine-stone / also Wine and their Spirits from the vegetable kingdom.

The philosophers <note>The "Philosophi" refers to the long tradition of alchemists and natural philosophers who sought to understand the hidden laws of nature.</note> report to us that nature is divided into three kingdoms / into the mineral, vegetable, and animal. Within the mineral [kingdom] are placed all manner of precious and base stones / all minerals / and metals. Within the vegetable / everything that grows out of the earth. And within the animal / humans / livestock / and everything that has a living breath. Of the mineral kingdom, a small amount has already been treated. Now follows the vegetable / and within the same, a discussion of wine and wine-stone <note>The hard crust of potassium bitartrate that forms in wine barrels, highly valued by alchemists as a "fixed salt."</note> / and of their comparison / with the heavenly and earthly suns / and because Sendivogius <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636) was a renowned Polish alchemist; "tract. 8" refers to the eighth treatise of his influential work *The New Chemical Light*.</note> in his eighth treatise reports: that the salts <note>original: *Salia*</note> are first and foremost to be observed in the first two kingdoms, the mineral and the vegetable / from which / as shall follow later / the animal is by no means to be excluded.

The heavenly sun has a correspondence with gold; which is attributed to the sun’s influences. Gold has a correspondence with the human heart / for its beautiful color gladdens the same. The heart, however / has a correspondence with wine / for it strengthens the same / refreshes and restores it / and makes it joyful /

### On the Animal Stone.

FIRST of all, there are two **Animal Stones** / one that is made from human urine and is called the **Spirit of Urine** <note>original: *Spiritus Urinæ*</note>. ### Nitrum, Saltpeter.

Saltpeter or *nitrum* <note>original Latin: "Nitrum"</note>, in Hebrew *neter* <note>original Hebrew: "NETER"</note> from *natar* <note>original: "Natar"</note>, meaning to loosen or dissolve <note>original Latin: "solvere"</note>, also called *hem alumen* <term>alumen: traditionally referring to alum, but here used by the author to categorize types of astringent mineral salts</term>, is also an animal salt—especially that which is dug out from cattle and sheep stalls. Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), the famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note>, part 1, folio 1073.

Saltpeter is nothing other than a cold salt which can endure no fire; it cannot remain if the fire is too great for it. Saltpeter can well endure a steady, even heat—for instance, on a warm stove it can withstand the heat—but if it is overtaken by a greater heat, it gives a thrust and heaves itself up <note>a reference to saltpeter's explosive potential when heated or ignited</note>. And the more it is enclosed, the harder it strikes. Saltpeter is nothing other than a spiritual essence and the excrement of all salts; it is of a hermaphroditic nature <term>hermaphroditic nature: in alchemy, a substance possessing dual or balanced qualities, appearing as neither fully one thing nor another</term>. It is not truly a salt, and not truly a sulfur. Theophrastus, part 1, folio 340.

Our saltpeter is not like the saltpeter of the Ancients, which was earthy; ours, however, is airy. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of 'Natural History'</note>, book 31, chapter 10. Theophrastus writes that saltpeter is a cold salt, and is also...

### XXIII.
### Silver Marcasite, Bismuth.

### XXIV.

### On Golden Marcasite, Zinc, Spelter, or Indian Tin.

Just as **bismuth**<note>original: *Wißmuth*.</note> makes **brass**<note>original: *Messing*.</note> resemble silver and derives its name from that, and **zinc** colors **copper** to resemble gold: so, without doubt, its name was drawn from this fact, leading it to be titled **Golden Marcasite**<note>original: *Marchasitam auream*; while we now know marcasite as iron sulfide, early modern miners used the term for various shiny metallic ores, including zinc ores like sphalerite.</note>. However, neither of these dyes or **tinctures**<note>original: *tingiret*; the alchemical process of changing the color and nature of a metal.</note> anything to be fire-resistant unless the Art of Nature comes to its aid. This mineral is otherwise also called **Magnesia**<note>In alchemical terms, "Magnesia" was a broad term for a "mother" substance or a mineral with magnetic/attractive properties, not specifically modern magnesium.</note>, and is subject to the **influence of Jupiter**<note>original: *Influenz Jovis*; Jupiter is the planetary correspondence for tin.</note>; and at the same time, because of its distance from the Sun, it is assigned to Jupiter just as **Silvery Marcasite**<note>original: *Marchasita argentea*; likely referring to bismuth or white iron pyrites.</note> is. It is an **intermediate mineral**<note>original: *Mittel-Mineral*; a substance categorized between stones and true metals.</note>, originating from **Sulfur and Mercury**<note>According to the "Sulfur-Mercury theory," all metals were thought to be composed of these two principles in varying degrees of purity and fixation.</note>. Its sulfur is volatile, poisonous, combustible, and foul-smelling; however, its mercury is **fixed**<note>Stable and resistant to heat.</note> and fire-resistant. Yet, because of the great amount of sulfur, it is carried upward in a strong fire, and the good is taken along with the evil. **Morienus**<note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist.</note> calls **Jupiter** [tin] a **pure metal**<note>original: *metallum purum*.</note>. But **Albertus Magnus, Book 5**<note>Referring again to *De mineralibus*.</note>...

### XXV.

### On the Stone Amianthus or Federweiß.

The stone Amianthus <note>original: *Lapis Amianthus*</note>, or Federweiß <note>literally "feather-white," a historical name for asbestos due to its fibrous, white appearance</note> is a mineral salt; and as Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> reports: it is primarily found on the island of Cyprus, where pillars and cloths are made from it. These were used for display and, when thrown into the fire, did not burn, but rather emerged more beautiful and shining. It is a species of alum <note>a group of hydrated double sulfate salts, often used as an astringent or in dyeing</note>, of which there are four kinds found in the apothecary: such as Rock Alum <note>original: *Alumen Rupeum* or *Rochæ*</note>, also called Roman Alum; Feathered Alum <note>original: *Alumen Plumosum*</note> or Amianthus stone, the aforementioned Federweiß, also called "Eternal Light" <note>referring to its use as a permanent wick for lamps</note> or "Earth Flax" <note>original: *Erdflachs*</note>. Regarding this, it is fabled that it grows from the hair of the Salamander <note>A mythical creature believed to live in and endure fire; its "hair" was a common metaphor for asbestos fibers</note>, because it does not burn in the fire, just like the Salamander.

The third alum is Sugar Alum <note>original: *Alumen Sacharinum*</note>, and the fourth is Slaty Alum <note>original: *Alumen scissile*</note>. Among these, the Slaty Alum is said to be the best, as Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> reports in Book 5, Chapter 3 of *On Metallic Things* <note>original: *De rebus Metallicis*</note>; especially when it is fresh, beautiful white like silver, with an astringent <note>literally "hard pulling to itself"</note> taste, foul-smelling, and free of stone. He says all of these should be easy to dissolve <note>original: *solviren*</note>, which cannot be said of the Feathered Alum, because it cannot be worked upon without a mastery <note>original: *Masterium*, likely referring to a specific alchemical process or secret solvent</note>. #### How the Amianth Stone <term>Lapis Amiantus: a fibrous, fire-resistant mineral, often called "mountain flax" or asbestos</term> is to be prepared.

Among the philosophers, lest the **Spirit** <note>In alchemy, "Spirit" refers to the volatile, elusive part of a substance that easily evaporates</note> fly away from them,
There has been, both now and in times past, the greatest care.
That which Nature has fixed in her own bosom,

Back into its very first principle. <note>The alchemical process of "reduction" or returning a substance to its most basic, elemental state</note>
Indeed, we have learned to prepare many **solvents** <term>Menstrua: the plural of menstruum, a term for a solvent used to dissolve or extract substances</term> through art,
But they do not take up every subject indiscriminately.
For although the same **Salt** is easily joined to a like **Salt**,
A distinction is nevertheless seen between them:
The solvent for **Silver** <note>original: *Argentum*</note> keeps its own, and the solvent for **Gold** <note>original: *Aurum*</note> holds its own;
Yet this **Salt** of ours addresses both of them at once.

# XXVII.

# Regarding Mirror-Stone, Talc, Arabic Stone, Cat-Silver, and Venetian Soap.

The **Arabic Stone** <note>original: *Arabische Stein*; *Lapis Arabicus*</note> is like speckled ivory, as **Dioscorides** <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD)</note> teaches, and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> (Book 36, Chapter 21) mentions it. Its use is as a tooth powder and to dry the flow of the **golden vein** <term>Golden vein: a historical medical term for hemorrhoids</term>. Much has been disputed by scholars, and is still disputed today, regarding what this stone actually is. However, if one considers the matter correctly, the **Arabic Stone** is nothing other than **Mirror-Stone** <note>original: *Spiegelstein*; *Lapis specularis*</note>, or **Moon-stone** <note>original: *Lapis Lunæ*</note>, **Mary’s Ice** <note>original: *Glacies Mariæ*; *unser Frauen Eis*</note>, known in German as **Spar-glass** <note>original: *Sperglaß*; refers to selenite or mica, which can be split into thin, transparent sheets</note>. It is a species of **Talc**, which is also called **Venetian Soap** <term>Venetian Soap: while usually a luxury soap, here it refers to talc's soapy feel and its use in cosmetics and medicinal preparations</term>.

In olden times, windows were made from this stone, with light wood placed between the pieces instead of lead. It is still used for large lanterns instead of other glass or horn. **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note> and **Dioscorides** call this Mirror-Stone **Aphroselinum** <note>original: *Aphroselinum*; from the Greek for "moon-foam"</note>, because at night it reflects the image of the moon. This Mirror-Stone is called the **Arabic Stone** for this reason: because it

# Dear Reader!

The aforementioned author of the *Saturnian Kingdom* has appended to his works several philosophical conclusions which indicate certain measures and ways to prepare the Stone <note>original: *Lapidem*, referring to the Philosopher's Stone</note>, as well as, finally, the actual practice <note>original: *Praxin*</note> of the Art. So that these should not remain behind or be considered useless, it has been deemed good to append them at the end of this little book and to add them here as a complement <note>original: *Complemento*</note> and addition. B. V. <note>The initials B. V. likely stand for Basilius Valentinus.</note>

---

## Several Conclusions.

1. Nature has left behind an imperfect thing, in that it has formed not the Stone <note>original: *Lapidem*</note>, but rather its matter <note>original: *Materi*</note>, which is hindered by accidental circumstances so that it cannot perform what the Stone can accomplish after its preparation. <note>This refers to the alchemical belief that the "Great Work" completes a process that Nature started but could not finish on its own.</note>

2. The substance <note>original: *Substanz*</note> and essence of that which is sought is entirely identical to that which is made from it.

3. This same equality is equal in kind <note>original: *Geschlecht*; here meaning genus or species</note>, not divided or numerical.

<meta>catchword: 4. Of</meta>

In this manner, if the work is carried out diligently according to weight, you will not easily go astray, which from...

<note>Philosophical Niter (Saltpeter) was considered by alchemists to be a "universal salt" or a celestial spirit captured in mineral form, essential for the animation of the Stone.</note>

### Concerning the Fixed Salt

Take the remaining earth <note>the residue left over from the previous distillation</note>, <term>calcine: to roast or burn a substance to a fine powder at high heat</term> it in an open fire to an ash for 12 hours. From this, extract the salt through <term>leaching: the process of washing the soluble salt out of the ash using water</term>, boiling, and <term>dissolving</term> <note>original: "Solvirung"</note>. Repeat this process and evaporate the liquid until you obtain a crystalline, transparent salt.

### The Joining of the Three Salts

Combine the fixed and the volatile salt; gradually pour the <term>spirit of nitre: a potent acid, typically nitric acid, distilled from saltpeter</term> <note>original: "Nitergeist"</note> upon them, and they will mix and turn into water. This water is the triumphant <term>Philosophical Mercury</term> <note>original: "Philosophische Mercurius"; not common quicksilver, but a purified "first matter" sought by alchemists</note> and the <term>Universal Solvent</term> <note>original: "Menstruum Universale"</note>, which is capable of dissolving all metals and even precious stones: for it is very fiery.

### The Preparation of the Universal Work

Take ten parts of the Universal Solvent and one part of the purest gold, beaten thin. Place it in a <term>flask</term> <note>original: "Kolben"; a round-bottomed glass distillation vessel</note>, and the solvent will immediately dissolve the gold. When the gold has been entirely <term>unlocked: a term for breaking down a metal into its constituent spiritual and physical parts</term>, a small amount of earth will remain at the bottom of the glass; let it stand overnight. One can also filter it into a <term>vial</term> <note>original: "Phiol"</note>, which can afterwards be <term>hermetically: an airtight seal, traditionally made by melting the glass neck of a vessel shut</term> sealed and kept safely in the inner sphere of the <term>athanor: a specialized alchemical furnace designed to provide steady, slow heat over long periods</term>.

## The Use of the Philosophical <term>Athanor</term> for this Work.
<note>An Athanor is a specialized furnace designed by alchemists to provide a steady, uniform heat over long periods without needing constant attention.</note>

There are three spheres in the Athanor: the first is the largest and is solid; the middle one is perforated at the top so that the steam may pass through; the third is made of oak wood, in which the <term>putrefaction</term> is carried out by the steam-fire.
<note>Putrefaction (German: *Fäulung*) is the essential first stage of the "Great Work," where the raw material is broken down and "dies" to be reborn.</note>
In the first sphere, there should be enough water, which, when it evaporates, must be replaced with more warm water. This stage of putrefaction is completed in forty or forty-five days, during which the blackness, known as the <term>Raven’s Head</term>, usually appears.
<note>Original: *Raben-Haupt*. This symbolizes the *nigredo* stage, where the matter turns deep black, signifying the successful beginning of the transformation.</note>
When the putrefaction is complete, remove the wooden sphere, as the water is no longer needed. Place it instead in the perforated sphere, which is filled with ashes; the degree of the fire should be so hot that it does not hurt the finger. Then, within 50 days, various colors will appear, which are called the <term>Peacock’s Tail</term>, and finally the Green color alone.
<note>Original: *Pfauen-Schwanz*. This refers to the *cauda pavonis* stage, an iridescent phase where the material displays many colors before settling into a single hue.</note>

After this, take the glass and place it in the largest sphere filled with sand, so that the sand covers the sealed glass with its material. Close the <term>Athanor</term>, stoke the fire underneath to a heat that a finger cannot endure; thus, within 50 days, it will become entirely white.
<note>The text here uses "Atkanor," a likely typographical error for Athanor.</note>
Continue with this degree of fire until the material turns yellow, which will happen within 30 or at most 50 days.

### The Multiplication
<note>Original: *Die Vermehrung*. The stage of the alchemical process where the potency and quantity of the Stone are increased.</note>

Take one part of your red fixed powder and ten parts of the menstruum, put them together in a phial, seal it hermetically, place it in the <term>athanor</term> <note>The steady-heat furnace described on the previous page.</note>, and proceed in all steps as before, until the blackness appears in the wooden sphere, the various colors in the second, and the red color in the first.

In this way, one can multiply the substance for a second and third time as desired.

### From a letter of Edward Kelley, of England, given at Trebona on June 20, 1507.

Our gold and silver; Sun and Moon, the active and the passive, is not that which we touch with our hands, but a golden and silver water, a <term>Hermaphrodite</term> <note>In alchemy, a "hermaphrodite" (or Rebis) represents a substance that combines both the male (sulfur/hot) and female (mercury/cold) principles in one body.</note>, which, when you extract it from a perfect and imperfect metallic body, you will have a water of life, a stinking <term>Asa</term> <note>original: "Asa"; likely referring to Asafoetida, used here to describe the pungent, sulfurous smell of the raw alchemical material.</note> and the <term>Green Lion</term> <note>The "Green Lion" is a famous symbol for the raw, acidic mineral or "vitriol" capable of dissolving gold.</note>, in which are all colors, but primarily two: white and red. Regarding the earth, there is no need to worry, provided that (as <term>Guido</term> <note>Likely referring to Guido de Montanor, a 15th-century alchemist often cited for his authority on the "fixed" nature of the philosophical earth.</note> testifies) it is fixed; for the <term>Elixir</term> is prepared above all fixed things. But especially take care, if you wish to dwell in the oldest and noblest philosophy, that you concern yourself with nothing else but the fixed earth and the persistent metallic water: and do not seek these in common gold and silver, or in any perfectly composed piece. ### From a letter from the same place
#### written on the 9th of August
#### Year [15]87.

The philosophers all conclude that the Stone is nothing other than the **animated mercury**: which, if it is not animated, is useless for their work. Likewise, while it is in its mercurial form, before it is animated, you should be certain that it is of no use. For this woman (that I may clearly reveal it to you) is a viscous water, drawn from the **entrails of Jove** <note>In alchemical symbolism, "Jove" or Jupiter refers to the metal Tin.</note>, namely from the **white lead** <note>original: "weissen Bley"; in this context, it refers to tin, distinguished from "black lead" (Saturn).</note>, which is moist and wets the finger. When you add the **gold-body** <note>The physical metal gold, used as the "seed" or "ferment" in the process.</note> to this, according to the correct weight, it will quickly unite with such in a congealed state, and the gold will be transformed into a clear mineral water. For the water will **dissolve** <note>original: "aufsolviren"</note> the gold in a minute, and through this dissolution the water solidifies; thus the dissolution of the one becomes the **coagulation** <note>The process where a liquid turns into a solid or semi-solid state.</note> of the other in an instant. This compound is the <term>animated mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurius animatus"; mercury that has been "awakened" or activated by a metallic seed, making it the primary matter for the Stone.</note>, from which alone all colors grow; for from this the colored ore is formed. The governance of the fire, however, is nothing other than child’s play.

## From the 15th of November [15]89.

You have both **luminaries** <note>In alchemical texts, the "Luminaries" typically represent the Sun and Moon, which symbolize Gold and Silver.</note>, and if you remember, the best instruction on how you should proceed with such things. And so that I may tell you much with a single word: mix the water with water and **digest** <note>original: "digerire"; the process of heating a substance slowly in a sealed vessel, often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen.</note> it in a steamy cloud, and you will not easily fail.

->*Oluf Borch, in his Dissertation on the Origin and Progress*<-
->*of Chemistry.*<- <note>original Latin: "Olaus Borrichius, in, de Ortu & progressu Chemiæ, dissertatione." Borch (1626–1690) was a Danish polymath and chemist.</note>

Paracelsus speaks very well when he says that the heavens are the origin and the ore-mines of the metals. While I am considering this rightly, there comes to my memory a singular **experiment** <note>original: "Experiment"</note> which that excellent man, **Kenelm Digby** <note>original: "Renemus Digbæus"; Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665) was a famous English courtier and natural philosopher known for his "powder of sympathy."</note>, the Chancellor of the King of Denmark in London, shared with me. I was staying, he said, in **Paris** during the time of **Cromwell** <note>Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England; Digby lived in exile in France during much of the English Civil War and Commonwealth.</note>, who was then punishing my fatherland; and to drive away the sorrowful memory of such an evil state, I amused myself with chemical **recreations** <note>original: "Erquisctungen"; literally "refreshments" or "delights," here referring to the intellectual joy of laboratory work.</note>. It then happened that an experienced man often filled my ears with the metallic virtues of the **Arcueil** <note>original: "Arcevilischen"; referring to Arcueil, an area south of Paris known for its limestone and ancient aqueducts.</note> earth. I let the desire overcome me and traveled to **Arcueil** (lying a short mile away from **Paris**).

<header>Addition.</header>

I ordered that about 20 pounds of such **reddish earth** should be dug up for me, which I also took with me into the city. On the following day, I divided it into 12 equal parts and spread them out in shallow earthenware vessels in the open air on the **attic** <note>original: "Soler"; a loft or upper room of a house often used for drying or storage.</note> of my house, placed under a small wooden roof so that they stood protected from the rain and wind. I also ordered that the material must be moistened daily with a small amount of rainwater. After one month had passed, I first took out the earthy material of the first **crucible** <note>original: "Tiegel"; here referring to the earthenware vessels used for the experiment.</note> and let it boil in more rainwater, and finally with a strong fire. When such water was filtered and became somewhat thicker after a gentle evaporation of the remaining moisture, there finally appeared on the bottom true signs of a real **vitriol** <note>original: "Vitriols"; a sulfate mineral, typically green or blue, used in various alchemical processes.</note> which manifested clearly in its color, taste, and angular shape. Furthermore, I continued with the moistening of the other crucibles, and when I performed the aforementioned work with the following vessels at the end of the second month, I found true **sulfur**. Likewise: in the third month, **lead** was produced for me; in the fourth, **tin**; in the fifth, **iron**; and in the sixth, I obtained **copper**, in which thin **silver fibers** <note>original: "Silberfeſerlein"; delicate, hair-like filaments of metallic silver.</note> were to be seen. An approaching thunderstorm knocked over the remaining six crucibles, so that I could not observe the subsequent results.

->E N D.<-
